meta.title: Pharmy Case Study: One Searchable Clinical Trial Platform | Viesigners
meta.description: How Charles-Erick BG led the UX of one searchable clinical trial platform and tested a two-step form on real traffic.

sections.h1: Turning scattered trial microsites into *a searchable platform built to recruit more participants*
sections.alt: Clinical trial search interface with results listed beside a map

sections.caption: The hub: search by condition and location, with results on a map. Visuals refreshed by me in 2025.
sections.lead: With the O2Web team, I led the UX and CRO of a clinical trial platform, from analysis to the winning version: 48% more visitors reached the form, contact requests came from prequalified people, and the client got a data-driven roadmap.

items.t: A large global pharmaceutical company. Pharmy is a fictional name; the real one is under NDA.
Get more qualification forms from potential trial participants.
UX and CRO expert, leading the UX and CRO.
I worked mainly with a consultant hired by the client. He approved the work, and the client made the final decisions.
Analysis, hypothesis, A/B methodology, measurement, information architecture and interface recommendations through wireframes. I also advised the graphic designer, who created the final UI.
more visitors reached the qualification form: 5.6% to 8.3% of visits.
more qualification forms sent per visit: 1.95% to 2.34%.
items.note: Note: small sample, not statistically significant.

items.t: data-driven next tests for the client, drawn from analytics and session recordings.

sections.label: The problem
sections.h2: Two problems kept people *from joining a trial*
prose: **People needed to trust the process before searching for a trial.** The client’s focus groups started this project. They showed that people were missing the information they needed to trust the platform and the process, and to decide to join. Distance mattered too: people had to go on site, so they needed a clinic close enough to reach. Yet each study had its own microsite, so the same general information was repeated on each one and harder to maintain.

**The qualification form felt very long.** My audit of the form showed the second problem: people didn’t fill it in and left, and the client relied only on those who finished it. The client’s team also lost time managing unqualified leads.

steps.p: Group the microsites in one searchable platform, like Airbnb for clinical trials, with the general information people needed in one place. That would also make updates easier for the client’s team.

steps.h: Test the page and the form on real traffic
steps.p: My audit of the qualification form led me to suggest a two-step version. We tested it with a study page that regrouped the key content around people’s main objections, against the existing version.

sections.label: Approach
prose: I started from the Google Analytics and Hotjar data, then framed the test hypothesis, wrote the A/B methodology and set the indicators and measurement plan with the client’s team.

I guided the project team through inspiration, ideation, prototyping and technical validation, and produced the information architecture and wireframes. The focus groups were run by the client before the project; I built on their findings.

items.h: Split a long form in two steps to keep people in the funnel
items.p: The form became a prescreener first, then contact details for people who qualified.

notes.v: The existing version with its one-step form, against the version with the regrouped study page and the two-step form I proposed.
My audit pointed to a long form that people left before finishing. A first step without personal details would ask less up front, and keep people in the funnel.

More build work: a way to go back a step, and saving the data after step 1 instead of sending everything at once. Of the people who reached the form, a smaller share sent it: 28% instead of 35%. Across all visits, submissions still rose.

items.h: Give people who don’t qualify a reason to stay
items.p: People who didn’t qualify could join a community through the newsletter.

notes.v: The newsletter kept them in the loop, so the client could reach them again and convert them later.
No downside noted for the client.

items.h: Answer objections before asking people to search
items.p: The homepage was designed to convince, not just inform. It made people feel part of a growing community and not alone, so they’d want to participate. A button then led to the search.

notes.v: If people have objections, they won’t act. The focus groups showed what was missing, so the right information had to come first.
Everyone passes through the homepage before searching. To limit that, the search stayed the most prominent item in the main menu.

sections.label: Design challenge
prose: Each microsite had its own navigation, and so did the search platform. The menu had to stay appealing, uncluttered and intuitive, even with both.

I explored two options: stacking the menus and hiding them on scroll, or swapping to the microsite menu with a clear back button. Stacked menus are harder on mobile and add cognitive load. Swapping is more mobile-first, but needs an intuitive way back. [À FOURNIR : which option shipped?]

sections.label: What real users did
sections.h2: What the A/B test *showed, and what it didn’t*

reads.p: Version B did better at convincing people to check their eligibility, a borderline significant result on this sample. It also sorted people: 47% of its submissions came from prequalified candidates, who then shared contact details, while the others could join the community.

On this small sample, the +20% isn’t statistically significant. Clicks on the form buttons also trended the other way, so some people may have reached the form directly. The report also flags test visits and configuration bugs. I flagged the sample size at the time, and the project moved forward.
Version B changed the study page and the form together, so the test can’t credit either one alone. It ran for three months. The numbers come from Google Analytics.

Hotjar recordings suggested friction on some prescreener fields, while qualified people filled in the contact form easily. On the not-qualified page, people mostly read the title and left. The client’s focus groups shaped the project, but the design itself wasn’t tested in moderated sessions.

sections.label: Outcome
prose: The platform went live, and the A/B test ran on real traffic. My report recommended keeping version B. It was a test for the client, and I don’t know whether they kept it.
My final report proposed the next tests: fewer calls to action on the study page, simpler prescreener fields, and a shorter not-qualified page with the community form at the top.
Today I’d push for more traffic or a longer test. It ran for three months, but too few people reached the forms to confirm the completion result.

I’d also turn the form into a multi-step wizard. The contact step would be sent as soon as people moved to step 2, and the qualification questions would be split into smaller chunks, so the form feels lighter and less intimidating.

On the homepage, I’d add a section right under the banner that builds empathy with people living with these conditions. It would show that we understand their situation before talking about the solution: joining the community of study participants.
